guides.title: Underperformance
guides.whenToUse: The quality or amount of someone's work is below the expected standard, deadlines are being missed, or informal feedback hasn't led to improvement.
before: Be clear on the standard expected and where it was set out (job description, objectives, previous 1:1s).
Gather 2–3 specific, recent examples with dates and the impact each had.
Consider whether training, tools, workload or unclear priorities could be part of the cause.
Think about whether health, personal circumstances or a disability could be a factor.
Check your company's performance or capability policy. Is this an informal conversation or a formal stage?
Decide what improvement looks like and a realistic timescale.
Book a private room or call with 30–45 minutes. Avoid Friday afternoons or the day before someone's holiday.
opening: "I want to talk about how [area of work] has been going. I've noticed some things I'm concerned about, and I want to help get it back on track."
"This is an informal conversation. The aim is to understand what's happening and agree how I can support you."

sayIt.line: Before I share what I've noticed, how do you feel things have been going?
The standard for [task] is [standard]. Over the last [period] it's been [what happened]. I want to understand why, so we can fix it together.
What's one thing I could do differently that would make the biggest difference for you?

during: Describe each example and its impact, using Situation, Behaviour, Impact.
Ask: "How do you think things have been going?"
Ask: "Is anything getting in the way – workload, training, tools, or anything outside work?"
Ask: "What would help you improve here?"
Agree clear, measurable expectations and a timescale.
Agree the support you'll provide and dates for check-ins.
Check understanding: "Can you sum up what we've agreed, so I know I've explained it clearly?"

responses.theySay: "No one told me that was the standard."
responses.youCould: Acknowledge it if that's fair. Make the standard clear now and agree to measure from today.
Explore it properly and reprioritise if that's fair, but keep the expected standard clear.
"I'm happy to look at that separately, but today I want to focus on your work and how I can help."

donts: Don't generalise ("You're always…", "You never…").
Don't compare them with colleagues.
Don't raise problems that have never been mentioned before as if they're long-standing.
Don't speculate about health or diagnose anything.
Don't threaten formal action. If you need to explain the process, do it factually.
hrTriggers: The employee mentions a health condition, disability, stress or mental health.
You're thinking about moving to a formal performance or capability process.
The employee raises a grievance or says they're being treated unfairly or discriminated against.
The issue has already been discussed informally and hasn't improved.
after: Send the summary within 24 hours.
Put the agreed check-ins in your diary (weekly or fortnightly).
Provide the support you promised.
Review at the end of the timescale, and recognise improvement when you see it.

summary.prompt: The standard expected, the examples I shared and their impact.

guides.title: Lateness and timekeeping
guides.whenToUse: An employee is regularly arriving late, taking long breaks or leaving early.
before: Check the facts: dates and times over a set period (e.g. the last 4–6 weeks).
Check their contracted hours and any flexible arrangements already agreed.
Look for a pattern (e.g. Mondays, school-run times) that might suggest a cause.
Consider caring responsibilities, transport problems or health.
Check your company's timekeeping or attendance policy.
opening: "I wanted to have a quick word about timekeeping. You've been late on [number] occasions over the last [period], and I wanted to understand what's going on."

sayIt.line: I've noticed you've been late a few times recently, on [dates]. Is everything OK?
Your start time is [time]. I need you here by then because [reason]. Can we agree that from tomorrow?
If something's making mornings difficult, tell me. There may be options we can look at properly.

during: Share the dates. Be factual, not accusatory.
Ask: "Is there anything behind this that I should know about?"
Explain the impact on the team or customers.
Restate the expected start and finish times.
If there's a genuine reason, explore options (e.g. a temporary change, or a formal flexible working request).
Agree the expectation and a review period.

responses.youCould: Show understanding. Explain that they can make a flexible working request, and point them to the Flexible working guide (G13).

responses.theySay: "I make the time up at the end of the day."
responses.youCould: Explain why start times matter in this role (cover, customers, meetings), or agree a trial of different hours.

donts: Don't raise it in front of colleagues.
Don't assume you know the reason.
Don't informally agree a permanent change to hours. Use the proper process.
hrTriggers: The lateness is linked to health or a disability.
Caring needs may lead to a flexible working request.
There's no improvement after an informal discussion (a possible formal stage).
You suspect alcohol or drug misuse.
after: Send the summary.
Monitor timekeeping over the agreed period.
Recognise improvement and close the matter if things are resolved.

summary.prompt: The dates discussed, the expected start/finish times and any reasons given.

guides.title: Behaviour and conduct
guides.whenToUse: An employee has behaved in a way that falls below expected standards, for example being rude to colleagues or customers, using inappropriate language or breaking a workplace rule.

escalation.headline: Contact HR first if this could be serious
escalation.stop: STOP if this could be serious (gross) misconduct, such as harassment, bullying, discrimination, violence, theft, fraud, a data breach or being under the influence at work. Contact HR before speaking to the employee.
escalation.triageIntro: Answer for yourself. Your answers are not saved and are not a clearance to go ahead.
triage: Could this involve harassment, bullying or discrimination?
Could this involve violence, theft, fraud, a data breach, or alcohol or drugs at work?
Could a formal disciplinary process follow, or has the employee raised a grievance?
escalation.ifYes: Stop here and speak to HR before you talk to the employee about it. Don't investigate, reach a view or promise confidentiality.
escalation.ifNo: Even if none of these apply, speak to HR first if anything could become formal. The guide below is for minor, informal issues.
escalation.holdingIntro: If it's raised with you before you've spoken to HR, you could say:
holding: Thank you for telling me. I'm taking this seriously, and I want to make sure it's handled properly, so I'm going to get advice before we go any further.
I can't promise to keep this completely confidential, but I'll only share it with the people who need to know to deal with it.
I'll come back to you by [date]. If anything changes before then, or you feel unsafe, tell me straight away.

before: For minor issues, establish exactly what happened: date, place, what was said or done, and who saw it.
Separate facts from hearsay and opinion.
Check the relevant policy (code of conduct, dignity at work).
Plan to hear their side before reaching any conclusion.
opening: "I want to talk about something that happened on [date]. I'd like to hear your side first, and then explain why it's a concern."

sayIt.line: Before I say anything else, I'd like to hear what happened from your point of view.
I don't think you meant it that way, but the impact was [impact], and that's what I need to address.
From now on, I need [expected behaviour]. Is there anything that would get in the way of that?

during: Describe what was seen or reported, factually.
Ask: "Can you talk me through what happened from your point of view?"
Listen without interrupting.
Explain the standard expected and why it matters.
Agree what happens next and what you expect from now on.

responses.youCould: Don't reveal names without HR advice. "I'd like us to focus on what happened and what needs to change."
Explain that how something is received matters as well as how it was meant, and restate the standard.

donts: Don't run an informal "investigation" into serious allegations. HR should lead.
Don't promise anyone confidentiality you can't keep.
Don't reach a conclusion before hearing their account.
Don't discuss the matter with other team members.
hrTriggers: BEFORE any conversation about possible harassment, bullying, discrimination, violence, theft, fraud, a data breach, or alcohol or drugs at work.
Whenever a formal disciplinary process might follow.
The employee alleges they're being treated unfairly or raises a grievance.
after: For informal matters, send the summary and monitor.
For anything formal, follow HR's guidance on records and letters. Don't send your own summary unless HR agrees.

summary.notice: If this matter may become formal, check with HR before sending a summary.
summary.prompt: What happened, your account, and the standard expected.

guides.title: Conflict between team members
guides.whenToUse: Two or more team members aren't getting on and it's affecting their work, the team or customers.
before: Plan to speak to each person separately first.
Be clear about the impact on work. That's your reason for getting involved.
Stay neutral. Don't arrive with a view on who's right.
Watch for signs of bullying, harassment or discrimination. If you see any, contact HR first.
opening: "I've noticed some tension between you and [colleague], and I'd like to help sort it out. Can you tell me how things look from your side?"

sayIt.line: I'm not here to decide who's right. I want to find a way for you both to work well together.
What's one thing [colleague] could do that would make working together easier? And one thing you could do?
Would you be willing to sit down together with me, with some simple ground rules?

during: In each one-to-one, listen, ask what's happened, what they need, and what they could do differently.
Ask if they'd be willing to meet together.
If you hold a joint meeting, set ground rules (each person speaks without interruption, focus on behaviours, not personalities).
Focus on the future: "What needs to happen for you to work well together?"
Agree specific working arrangements and a review date.

responses.youCould: Don't force it. Agree working arrangements separately, and consider HR or mediation.

donts: Don't take sides.
Don't force a joint meeting.
Don't repeat what one person told you in confidence without their agreement.
Don't ignore it and hope it goes away.
hrTriggers: There are allegations of bullying, harassment or discrimination.
Either person raises a formal grievance.
You think mediation is needed.
after: Send each person their own summary (only send a joint summary after a joint meeting).
Check in with each person after 2 weeks.

summary.prompt: The impact on work, your perspective and what we agreed about working together.

guides.title: Frequent short-term sickness absence
guides.whenToUse: An employee has had several short absences and they're starting to affect the team or have reached a trigger point in your absence policy.
before: Check the absence record: dates, reasons and total days over the period.
Check whether the absences have reached a trigger point in your policy.
Make sure return to work meetings were held and recorded.
Consider whether there could be an underlying condition, disability, pregnancy-related illness or work-related stress.
Find out whether Occupational Health (OH) or an Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) is available.
opening: "I wanted to talk about your absences over the last [period]. This isn't about doubting that you've been unwell. I want to understand whether there's anything behind it and how we can support you."

sayIt.line: I'm not questioning that you've been ill. I want to see whether there's anything we can do to help.
Is there anything that links these absences, or anything at work that's making things harder?
I want to be open with you: our policy says [trigger]. I'd much rather we find support that helps before it gets to that.

during: Share the record factually.
Ask: "Is there an underlying reason, or anything that connects these absences?"
Ask whether anything at work is contributing.
Explain the impact on the team.
Discuss support: OH referral, EAP, adjustments.
Explain your absence policy and what happens if absences continue, factually and without threat.

responses.theySay: "I have a condition I haven't mentioned."
responses.youCould: Thank them for telling you. Discuss support, consider an OH referral and contact HR.

donts: Don't ask for more medical detail than you need.
Don't suggest they're not genuinely ill.
Don't count pregnancy-related or disability-related absences in the usual way without HR advice.
Don't put medical details in the summary email.
hrTriggers: There may be a disability or long-term health condition.
Absences are pregnancy-related.
Work-related stress or an injury at work is mentioned.
A formal stage of your absence policy has been reached.
The absence becomes long-term (often defined as 4 weeks or more).
after: Send the summary (without medical details).
Make the OH referral if agreed.
Hold the review on the agreed date.

summary.prompt: The absence dates discussed, the support offered and the policy explained. No medical details.

guides.title: Mental health disclosure or concern
guides.whenToUse: An employee tells you they're struggling with their mental health, or you've noticed signs that they may be.
before: If you're starting the conversation, note the changes you've seen (behaviour and work, not a diagnosis).
Find a private, comfortable space and allow plenty of time, with no hard stop.
Know the support available: your Employee Assistance Programme (EAP), Occupational Health (OH), mental health first aiders, their GP, and crisis lines (e.g. Samaritans 116 123).
opening: "I've noticed you haven't seemed yourself lately. How are you doing?"
If they tell you something: "Thank you for telling me. I'm glad you felt able to."

sayIt.line: There's no pressure to talk now. If you'd like to, now or another time, I'm here.
Thank you for telling me. That can't have been easy. What would help most right now?
Who, if anyone, would you like me to share this with? I'll only tell people what they need to know.

during: Listen more than you talk. Silence is fine.
Ask open questions: "How is it affecting you at work?" "What would help right now?"
Ask what, if anything, they'd like shared, and with whom.
Discuss possible adjustments: temporary hours, workload, breaks, where they work.
Point them to support (EAP, GP, OH).
Agree when you'll next check in.

responses.youCould: Respect that. Explain who, if anyone, would need to know (e.g. HR to arrange adjustments). The exception is if there's a risk to their safety.
Don't push. "OK, but my door's open. If anything changes, I'm here." Check in again soon.

donts: Don't diagnose or give opinions about conditions.
Don't promise complete confidentiality if there's a risk to life.
Don't make assumptions about what they can or can't do.
Don't overwhelm them with solutions in the first conversation.
hrTriggers: URGENT: If they say they may harm themselves or others, don't leave them alone. Call 999 or help them contact a crisis line, then contact HR.
Adjustments involving changes to hours, duties or contract.
A long-term condition is mentioned (it may count as a disability under the Equality Act 2010).
Stress is caused or made worse by work.
after: Check in as agreed. Keep it regular and low-key.
Arrange the agreed adjustments.
Keep what they told you private.

summary.notice: Ask the employee whether they'd like a written summary. If they would, record only the support and actions agreed, not health details.
summary.prompt: The support and actions agreed. No health details.

guides.title: Bereavement
guides.whenToUse: An employee has lost someone close to them, both when they first tell you and when they return to work.
before: Check your bereavement or compassionate leave policy.
Be aware of statutory rights: reasonable time off for dependants, and parental bereavement leave for the loss of a child under 18 or a stillbirth after 24 weeks of pregnancy.
Think about what you can offer: leave, flexibility, a phased return.
opening: "I'm so sorry to hear about your [relationship]. Please don't worry about work right now. I want to make sure you have what you need."

sayIt.line: Please don't think about work right now. Take the time you need, and tell me what would help.
How would you like me to keep in touch while you're off? A message now and then, or would you rather contact me?
Welcome back. There's no right way to feel. If you need some flexibility, just say.

during: First conversation: keep it short and kind.
Ask how much time they think they need and explain what leave is available.
Ask whether and how they'd like the team told.
Agree how and how often they'd like to be contacted while they're off.
On their return: ask how they're doing, and offer a phased return or flexibility. Remind them about the Employee Assistance Programme (EAP), if you have one.

responses.youCould: Respect that, and make it clear they can change their mind at any time.

donts: Don't push for a return date in the first conversation.
Don't say "I know how you feel" or try to minimise their loss.
Don't share the news without their agreement.
Don't forget that anniversaries and key dates can be hard later on.
hrTriggers: Leave is needed beyond your policy.
It's the death of a child (parental bereavement leave applies).
Grief is affecting their health or attendance over a longer period.
after: Keep in touch as agreed.
Make a note to yourself of significant dates (e.g. anniversaries), but not in this app.

summary.notice: A full summary isn't usually appropriate after a bereavement conversation. This short version confirms only the leave and contact arrangements agreed.
summary.prompt: The leave and contact arrangements agreed.

guides.title: Menopause
guides.whenToUse: An employee tells you menopause symptoms are affecting them at work, or asks for support.
before: Check whether your company has a menopause policy or support.
Be ready to listen. You don't need to be an expert.
Know the common adjustments: temperature control or a fan, uniform changes, extra breaks, flexible hours, home working, access to rest areas.
opening: "Thanks for raising this with me. I'd like to understand how it's affecting you at work and what would help."

sayIt.line: Thanks for telling me. You only need to share what you're comfortable with.
What would make the biggest difference to you at work right now?
Let's try these changes and check in again in [time] to see how they're working.

during: Ask which symptoms affect their work, only as much as they want to share.
Ask what adjustments would help.
Agree what you can put in place and a date to review.
Point them to support: your Employee Assistance Programme (EAP), their GP, Occupational Health (OH) or any internal network.

responses.youCould: Reassure them it's a normal workplace conversation and they only need to share what they're comfortable with.

donts: Don't make jokes or assumptions.
Don't dismiss or play down symptoms.
Don't make comments about age.
hrTriggers: Adjustments would change their contract (hours, duties).
Symptoms are linked to absence or performance concerns.
There's a risk of discrimination. Menopause-related treatment can raise age, sex or disability discrimination issues.
after: Put the agreed adjustments in place.
Review on the agreed date.

summary.prompt: The adjustments and support agreed.

guides.title: Pregnancy announcement
guides.whenToUse: An employee tells you they're pregnant.
before: This conversation is usually started by the employee, so know the basics in advance.
Pregnant employees are protected from discrimination and unfavourable treatment.
They're entitled to paid time off for antenatal appointments.
A workplace risk assessment is needed.
HR will explain maternity leave and pay.
opening: "Congratulations! Thank you for letting me know."

sayIt.line: Congratulations! How are you feeling?
Who knows so far? When, and how, would you like the team to be told?
HR will be in touch about leave and pay. In the meantime, time off for appointments is absolutely fine.

during: Ask how they're feeling and whether they need anything now.
Ask who knows and whether or when they'd like the team told.
Explain the next steps: HR will be in touch about leave and pay, a risk assessment will be done, and time off for appointments is fine.
Ask them to let you know if their needs change.

responses.youCould: Reassure them that their pregnancy won't affect how they're treated, and that HR can answer detailed questions.

donts: Don't ask whether they plan to come back, or about childcare.
Don't make assumptions about workload, travel or promotion.
Don't share the news without their agreement.
Don't change their duties without discussing it with them and carrying out a risk assessment.
hrTriggers: Always tell HR, with the employee's agreement, so the risk assessment and maternity process can start.
The employee reports pregnancy-related illness or absence.
There are concerns about how they're being treated.
after: Let HR know.
Arrange the risk assessment.
Keep the news confidential until they're ready.

summary.prompt: Next steps agreed (HR contact, risk assessment, appointments).

guides.title: Personal hygiene
guides.whenToUse: An employee's personal hygiene is noticeably and consistently affecting colleagues or customers.
before: Make sure it's a genuine, consistent issue, not a one-off or a single complaint.
Consider possible causes: a medical condition, medication, mental health, money worries, home circumstances or cultural factors.
Choose a completely private setting, ideally towards the end of the day.
Have support information ready, such as your Employee Assistance Programme (EAP).
opening: "There's something a bit sensitive I need to talk to you about. I'm going to be direct, because I think that's kinder than not saying anything. There have been times recently when there's been a noticeable body odour."

sayIt.line: This is a sensitive thing to raise. I'm telling you because I'd want someone to tell me.
Take a moment. I know this isn't easy to hear.
Is there anything going on that's making this harder? If there is, I'd like to help.

during: Be direct, brief and factual. Then pause and let them respond.
Ask: "Is there anything that might be contributing to this?"
Offer support if there's an underlying reason.
Agree next steps and reassure them it stays private.

responses.youCould: Give them a moment. "I know this isn't easy to hear. I'm raising it because I want to help."
Don't name anyone. "I've noticed it myself, and I wanted to raise it with you privately."

donts: Don't drop hints or leave anonymous notes or products.
Don't say "people have been complaining" or name colleagues.
Don't joke about it.
Don't drag it out.
hrTriggers: There may be a medical cause or disability.
You have concerns about their mental health or circumstances at home.
The employee becomes very distressed.
The issue continues after the conversation.
after: Monitor the situation discreetly.
If things improve, consider a brief, positive acknowledgement in private.

summary.notice: A written summary is optional. Consider whether it's needed.
summary.prompt: What we discussed and the support agreed.

guides.title: Giving feedback
guides.whenToUse: You want to give positive or developmental feedback about something specific.
before: Pick one specific situation.
Note the behaviour (what you saw or heard) and its impact.
Give it soon after the event.
Positive feedback can be given in public. Developmental feedback should be given in private.
Tip: use the SBI Feedback Builder in the Toolkit to prepare.
opening: "Have you got 10 minutes? I wanted to give you some feedback on [situation]."

sayIt.line: In [situation], you [behaviour]. That meant [impact]. Please keep doing that.
In [situation], you [behaviour]. The impact was [impact]. How did you see it?
What could you try differently next time?

during: Situation: "In yesterday's client meeting…"
Behaviour: "…you interrupted the client twice while they were explaining the issue…"
Impact: "…which meant we didn't fully understand their concern, and they seemed frustrated."
Ask: "How did you see it?"
Agree what to do next time (developmental), or say what you'd like them to keep doing (positive).

responses.youCould: Listen and ask for their perspective. You can accept that you see it differently, as long as the expectation is clear.

donts: Don't hide the message by sandwiching it between compliments.
Don't use vague labels ("unprofessional", "great job"). Be specific.
Don't give too much at once.
hrTriggers: Not usually needed. If the feedback is about conduct, use the Behaviour and conduct guide (G03).
after: Follow up on developmental feedback the next time the situation comes up.

summary.prompt: The situation, behaviour and impact, and what we agreed.

guides.title: Saying no to a request
guides.whenToUse: You need to turn down a request for something like training, particular leave dates, a project or a budget.
before: Be clear about why the answer is no.
Think about alternatives: a later date, a partial yes, or a different way to meet the need.
Check whether a formal process applies. Flexible working, statutory leave and disability adjustments must follow set procedures (see G13 or contact HR).
opening: "Thanks for asking about [request]. I've thought about it carefully and I'm not able to agree to it right now. I want to explain why."

sayIt.line: I've thought about it properly, and the answer is no for now. I want to explain why.
I know that's disappointing, and I appreciate you asking.
What would need to change for a yes is [condition]. Shall we look at that together?

during: Give the honest reason.
Acknowledge their disappointment.
Offer alternatives, or explain what would need to change for a yes.
Agree any next steps.

responses.youCould: Explain the difference in circumstances if you can, without discussing the colleague's details.

donts: Don't put it off or avoid the conversation.
Don't blame others ("HR won't let me") if it's your decision.
Don't promise a future yes you can't guarantee.
hrTriggers: The request is for flexible working, statutory leave (e.g. parental leave, time off for dependants) or an adjustment for a disability or health condition.
after: Follow up on any alternative you offered.

summary.prompt: The request, the reason for the decision and any alternatives offered.

guides.title: Flexible working request
guides.whenToUse: An employee has made, or wants to make, a request to change their hours, times or place of work.

escalation.headline: Contact HR before you respond
escalation.stop: Flexible working requests have legal time limits and a fixed list of reasons for refusal. Speak to HR and check your policy before the meeting, and always before you respond in writing.
escalation.triageIntro: Answer for yourself. Your answers are not saved and are not a clearance to go ahead.
triage: Is this a formal (statutory) request, or could it become one?
Are you thinking of refusing it, or only agreeing to part of it?
Could it be linked to a disability, or to a return from maternity, adoption or shared parental leave?
escalation.ifYes: Speak to HR before you meet or reply. Don't refuse or agree anything in the meeting, and don't put a decision in writing until HR has advised.
escalation.ifNo: Even so, check with HR before you respond in writing. Requests have legal time limits.
escalation.holdingIntro: If you need to respond before you have spoken to HR, you could say:
holding: Thanks for your request. I want to give it proper consideration, so I'm going to take advice and I'll come back to you by [date].
I can't give you a decision today, but I'll make sure it's looked at properly and within the time limits.

before: Check whether it's a formal (statutory) request. In the UK, employees can make a request from their first day of employment, up to two requests in any 12-month period.
The employer must consult the employee before refusing, and must make a decision (including any appeal) within two months unless an extension is agreed.
A request can only be refused for one of the eight statutory business reasons.
Review the request: what's being asked for, the impact on the team, and whether a trial period could work.
Contact HR and check your company's policy before the meeting.
opening: "Thanks for your request. I'd like to talk it through so I fully understand what you're looking for, and we can explore what might work."

sayIt.line: Talk me through what you're looking for and how you think it would work day to day.
You don't need to tell me why. I just want to find something that works for you and the team.
I'll consider it properly and give you a written decision by [date].

during: Understand exactly what they're asking for. They don't have to give a reason.
Discuss how it could work in practice and any concerns about impact.
Explore alternatives or a compromise.
Consider a trial period.
Explain the next steps and when they'll get a written decision.

responses.theySay: "Why do you need to know my reasons?"
responses.youCould: You don't need them. "You don't have to tell me. I just want to find something that works."

donts: Don't refuse in the meeting before considering it properly.
Don't ask intrusive questions.
Don't treat requests differently depending on the reason (e.g. childcare vs other reasons).
Don't agree a change informally without it being recorded. An accepted request is usually a permanent change to the contract unless a trial or end date is agreed.
hrTriggers: Always, before you respond in writing.
You're considering a refusal.
The request is linked to a disability (it may be a reasonable adjustment) or a return from maternity, adoption or shared parental leave.
after: Send the meeting summary.
Work with HR on the formal written decision. This is separate from the summary.

summary.prompt: What was requested, how it might work, alternatives discussed and the timescale for a decision.
summary.formNote: This is a meeting summary, not your formal decision.

guides.title: Pay rise request
guides.whenToUse: An employee asks for a pay rise.
before: Check the pay range for the role, their pay history, and when and how pay decisions are made.
Be clear about what you can and can't decide.
Think about their contribution and how it compares to the expectations of the role.
opening: "Thanks for raising this. I'd like to hear your case, and then I'll explain how pay decisions work here."

sayIt.line: Thanks for raising this. Tell me what you think justifies an increase.
I can't promise anything today. Pay decisions here are made [how and when].
If it's not possible now, let's agree what would need to happen for it to be possible.

during: Listen to their case in full.
Ask what they think justifies the increase.
Explain the process and timing honestly.
Be realistic about the likelihood.
If it's not possible now, agree what would need to happen (objectives, skills, responsibilities).
Agree when you'll get back to them.

responses.youCould: Thank them for being open. Don't react on the spot. Take advice before responding.

donts: Don't promise an increase you can't approve.
Don't discuss colleagues' pay.
Don't dismiss the request or treat them differently for asking.
hrTriggers: They raise equal pay concerns.
There's a counter-offer or a risk they'll leave.
The increase would take them outside the pay range.
after: Get back to them by the agreed date, even if it's just an update.

summary.prompt: Your request, the process explained and what happens next.

guides.title: Announcing change
guides.whenToUse: You need to tell your team or an individual about a change, such as a new process, a team restructure, an office move or new reporting lines.
before: Be clear about what's been decided and what's still open.
Know the reason for the change and be able to explain it simply.
Prepare answers to the questions you expect.
Time it so people hear it from you first, not through rumour.
If jobs, pay, hours, location or contracts could be affected, contact HR first. A formal consultation may be required.
opening: "I want to update you on a change that's coming to [team/process], and what it means for you."

sayIt.line: Here's what's changing, why it's happening, and when it takes effect.
Change can be unsettling. It's fine to have questions or worries, and I want to hear them.
I don't know yet. I'll find out and come back to you by [date].

during: Explain what is changing, why, when, and how it affects them.
Acknowledge how they might feel.
Invite questions.
Be honest when you don't know: "I don't know yet, but I'll find out and come back to you by [date]."
Explain the next steps and where to get support.

responses.youCould: If you don't know, say so honestly. Don't speculate. Find out and get back to them.

donts: Don't speculate or share rumours.
Don't make promises you can't keep.
Don't announce anything that puts roles at risk without the HR process in place.
Don't ignore people's feelings.
hrTriggers: There are any changes to terms and conditions, hours, pay or location.
Roles are at risk or redundancy is possible.
A transfer to another employer (TUPE) is involved.
after: Follow up on open questions by the date you promised.
Check in with individuals who seemed most affected.

summary.prompt: The change, the timing and the questions raised.
summary.formNote: A summary is optional for individual conversations.

guides.title: Grievance raised
guides.whenToUse: An employee tells you they want to raise a grievance, or puts a complaint about their work, their treatment or a colleague in writing.

escalation.headline: Contact HR before you respond to a grievance
escalation.stop: A grievance may need to follow your grievance procedure and the Acas Code of Practice. Listen and acknowledge it, but don't investigate or decide anything yourself, and contact HR before you respond in writing.
escalation.triageIntro: Answer for yourself. Your answers are not saved and are not a clearance to go ahead.
triage: Is the grievance about you, or about someone you manage closely?
Does it mention harassment, bullying, discrimination, whistleblowing or safety?
Has it been put in writing, or have they asked for it to be dealt with formally?
escalation.ifYes: Don't handle it yourself. Pass it to HR straight away, and don't discuss it with the person it's about.
escalation.ifNo: Even so, tell HR. An informal concern can still become a formal grievance.
escalation.holdingIntro: If you need to respond before you've spoken to HR, you could say:
holding: Thank you for raising this with me. I want to make sure it's handled properly, so I'll speak to HR and come back to you by [date].
I can't promise what the outcome will be, but I can promise it will be taken seriously.
If you'd like to put it in writing, you can, and you can ask for it to be dealt with formally.

before: Find your organisation's grievance policy and who handles grievances.
Note the date the concern was raised and how (in person, email or letter).
Check whether you're involved in the complaint. If you are, someone else must deal with it.
opening: "Thank you for telling me. I want to understand what's happened, and then make sure it goes to the right place."

sayIt.line: Take your time. Tell me what's happened and what you'd like to happen next.
I'm going to pass this to HR so it's handled fairly and in the right way. They'll be in touch by [date].
I'll only share this with the people who need to know to deal with it.

during: Listen and let them explain in their own words.
Ask what outcome they're hoping for.
Explain the next step: you'll involve HR, and they can put the grievance in writing if they want it handled formally.
Explain that they can be accompanied at a formal grievance meeting.

responses.theySay: "I don't want it to be formal."
responses.youCould: Respect that, but explain you still need to tell HR so it's handled properly. Let them know they can make it formal later.
Thank them for telling you. Don't defend yourself or discuss it. Explain that someone else will deal with it, and contact HR.

donts: Don't investigate or reach a view yourself.
Don't discuss the grievance with the person it's about.
Don't promise an outcome.
Don't treat them differently for raising it.
hrTriggers: Always, when a grievance is raised, and before you respond in writing.
The grievance is about you.
It involves harassment, discrimination, whistleblowing or safety.
after: Pass the details to HR the same day if you can.
Follow HR's guidance on records. Don't send your own summary of the grievance unless HR agrees.

summary.prompt: Only that they raised a concern, the date, and that you've passed it to HR.
summary.notice: Check with HR before sending anything in writing about a grievance.

guides.title: Harassment or bullying complaint
guides.whenToUse: An employee tells you they've been harassed, bullied or discriminated against at work, or you see it happen.

escalation.headline: Contact HR before you take any further step
escalation.stop: Harassment, bullying and discrimination complaints need HR to lead. Listen, check the person is safe, and contact HR. Don't investigate, confront the person accused or promise confidentiality.
escalation.triageIntro: Answer for yourself. Your answers are not saved and are not a clearance to go ahead.
triage: Is anyone at risk of harm, or do they feel unsafe at work right now?
Does it involve sexual harassment, violence or a threat?
Is the person accused their manager, someone senior, or you?
escalation.ifYes: Contact HR now. If anyone is in immediate danger, call 999. Agree with HR how to keep the person safe while it's looked into.
escalation.ifNo: Even so, contact HR before you do anything else. Complaints like this need a fair, independent process.
escalation.holdingIntro: While you contact HR, you could say:
holding: Thank you for telling me. I'm taking this seriously, and I'm going to get the right people involved so it's handled properly.
I can't promise to keep this completely confidential, but I'll only share it with the people who need to know.
Is there anything you need right now to feel safe at work?

before: Find a private place where you won't be overheard.
Know your HR contact and your organisation's dignity at work or harassment policy.
If you saw it happen, write down what you saw, with the date and time, for HR.
opening: "Thank you for coming to me. Take your time. I'm going to listen."

sayIt.line: I'm glad you told me. I'm not going to decide anything now; I'm going to make sure it's looked at properly.
Do you feel safe at work at the moment? Is there anything we need to change straight away?
I'm going to speak to HR today. They'll explain what happens next, and I'll check in with you by [date].

during: Listen without interrupting or questioning their account.
Note what they tell you in their own words, with dates if they give them.
Ask whether they feel safe and whether anything needs to change now, for example who they work with.
Explain that you'll involve HR, and what happens next as far as you know.

responses.youCould: Explain honestly that you can't keep it completely confidential, because it has to be dealt with properly, but you'll only share it with the people who need to know.

responses.theySay: "I don't want to make a fuss."
responses.youCould: Reassure them that raising it is the right thing to do, and that it will be handled carefully.

donts: Don't investigate or question witnesses yourself.
Don't confront or warn the person accused.
Don't say whether you believe it.
Don't promise confidentiality or a particular outcome.
Don't move the person who complained without their agreement and HR's advice.
hrTriggers: Always, straight away.
Anyone is at risk of harm. Also call 999 if the danger is immediate.
The person accused is senior, or is you.
after: Give HR your notes the same day.
Check in with the person who raised it, as agreed with HR.
Watch for any victimisation of the person who complained, and tell HR straight away.

summary.prompt: Only that they raised a concern and you've passed it to HR. Check with HR first.
summary.notice: Speak to HR before sending anything in writing about this.

guides.title: Suspected impairment at work
guides.whenToUse: You think an employee may be under the influence of alcohol or drugs at work, or unfit to work safely for another reason, such as medication or exhaustion.

escalation.headline: Safety first, then HR
escalation.stop: If someone may be unfit to work safely, stop them doing safety-critical work (such as driving or using machinery) straight away. Contact HR before any conversation about possible misconduct. If they seem seriously unwell, get medical help.
escalation.triageIntro: Answer for yourself. Your answers are not saved and are not a clearance to go ahead.
triage: Could they, or anyone else, be in danger if they carry on working?
Do they seem unwell, confused or injured?
Could this lead to disciplinary action?
escalation.ifYes: Make the situation safe first: stop the task, and call 999 or get first aid if they're unwell. Then contact HR before you talk about what's happened.
escalation.ifNo: Even so, speak to HR before you talk to them about possible alcohol or drug use.
escalation.holdingIntro: To keep everyone safe while you contact HR, you could say:
holding: I'm concerned you're not well enough to work safely right now, so I'm going to stop you working on [task] for now.
I'm not making any judgement about why. I just need to make sure you and everyone else are safe.
Let's get you home safely. We'll talk properly when you're back, and I'll be in touch by [date].

before: Check your organisation's drugs and alcohol policy, including any testing rules.
Ask a second manager or HR to be with you if you can.
Note what you've seen: behaviour, speech, smell, coordination, and the time and date.
opening: "I've noticed you don't seem yourself today, and I'm worried about you. Can we talk somewhere private?"

sayIt.line: I've noticed [what you observed], and I'm concerned about whether you're OK to work safely.
I don't want you to drive. Who can collect you, or shall I arrange a taxi?
If there's something going on, support is available, and you can talk to me or HR about it in confidence.

during: Describe what you've seen, factually.
Don't accuse or diagnose. Ask if they're OK, and whether they've taken any medication.
Stop them doing safety-critical work and arrange for them to get home safely, not by driving.
Mention support, such as your Employee Assistance Programme (EAP), if you have one.

responses.theySay: "I'm fine, I've just had a bad night."
responses.youCould: Acknowledge that. If you're still concerned about safety, explain that you need them to stop work today, and that you'll talk properly later.

responses.theySay: "I've got a problem and I need help."
responses.youCould: Thank them for telling you. Treat it as a health and support matter, mention the EAP or their GP, and contact HR about support.

donts: Don't let them drive or carry on with safety-critical work.
Don't search them or their belongings.
Don't accuse them or discuss it in front of others.
Don't send them home alone if they seem unwell.
hrTriggers: Always, before any conversation about possible alcohol or drug use.
Safety-critical work is involved.
They tell you about an addiction or a health condition.
after: Write down what you saw and what you did, and give it to HR.
Plan a return-to-work conversation with HR's advice.

summary.prompt: Only what's needed: that you were concerned about safety and what you agreed. Check with HR first.
summary.notice: Speak to HR before sending anything in writing about this.

guides.title: Redundancy or restructure
guides.whenToUse: Your organisation is planning changes that could put jobs at risk, change roles or reduce numbers, and you need to talk to your team or someone in it.

escalation.headline: Don't share anything until HR is ready
escalation.stop: Redundancy and restructuring have legal consultation requirements. Only share what HR has approved, at the time they agree. Don't speculate, make promises or select anyone yourself.
escalation.triageIntro: Answer for yourself. Your answers are not saved and are not a clearance to go ahead.
triage: Could any roles be at risk, or could terms (pay, hours or location) change?
Are you being asked about plans that haven't been announced?
Is anyone affected pregnant, on or just back from maternity, adoption or shared parental leave, or off sick?
escalation.ifYes: Speak to HR before you say anything. There may be rules about timing and consultation, and extra protection for some people.
escalation.ifNo: Even so, check your wording with HR before you talk to the team.
escalation.holdingIntro: If you're asked before HR is ready, you could say:
holding: I can't share any more at the moment. When I can, I will, and I'll tell you as soon as I'm able.
I don't know the answer yet. I'll find out and come back to you by [date].
I know this is unsettling. Please come and talk to me if you're worried.

before: Get HR's briefing, the approved message and the timetable.
Know what support is available, such as your Employee Assistance Programme (EAP).
Plan for people's reactions: allow time and a private space.
opening: "I want to update you on some proposed changes. I'll tell you what I know, what it could mean for you, and what happens next."

sayIt.line: These are proposals at this stage. There will be a consultation, and your views will be listened to.
It's completely understandable to feel worried. You can ask me anything, and if I don't know, I'll find out.
If you'd like to talk to someone outside the team, [support] is available.

during: Stick to HR's approved message.
Explain what is proposed, why, and the timetable.
Explain how consultation will work and who to contact.
Listen, and write down any questions you can't answer.

responses.youCould: Be honest. If you don't know, say so. Don't guess or reassure without the facts.
Explain that no decisions have been made and that there will be a fair process. Refer detailed questions to HR.

donts: Don't speculate or share rumours.
Don't make promises about who will be affected.
Don't talk about it before HR's agreed timing.
Don't discuss individuals with the team.
hrTriggers: Always, before any conversation.
Someone affected is pregnant, on or returning from family leave, or off sick.
Someone raises a grievance about the process.
after: Pass unanswered questions to HR.
Follow HR's guidance on written records and letters. Don't send your own summary unless HR agrees.
Check in with people individually.

summary.prompt: Only what HR has approved. Check with HR first.
summary.notice: Speak to HR before sending anything in writing about redundancy or restructuring.

guides.title: Poor team morale
guides.whenToUse: Your team seems flat, frustrated or disengaged, for example after a difficult period, a change or a heavy workload.
before: Look for patterns: workload, recent changes, absence, conflict or lack of recognition.
Decide whether to start with one-to-ones or a team conversation.
Be ready to listen rather than fix everything at once.
opening: "I've noticed the team seems under pressure lately, and I want to hear how things really are for you."

sayIt.line: I'd really like to hear what's working and what isn't. Nothing you say will be held against you.
Some of this may be down to me. What could I do differently?
Let's pick one or two things we can change in the next [period], and check back on them.

during: Ask open questions: what's going well, what's hard, and what would help.
Listen, and sum up what you hear without defending.
Agree one or two practical changes, with owners and dates.
Recognise effort and what's gone well.

responses.youCould: Acknowledge it. Agree something small you can change quickly, and report back on it.
Give people time. Offer other ways to share their views, such as one-to-ones.

donts: Don't get defensive or dismiss concerns.
Don't promise changes you can't deliver.
Don't single people out in a group.
hrTriggers: Morale problems involve bullying, harassment or discrimination.
Several people raise the same serious concern.
High absence or turnover suggests a wider problem.
after: Share what you heard and what will change.
Follow up the agreed actions by the date you set.
Keep checking in at 1:1s.

summary.prompt: What you heard and the changes you agreed.

guides.title: Managing a former peer
guides.whenToUse: You've been promoted to manage people who used to be your colleagues or friends at work.
before: Plan one-to-ones with each person early on.
Think about what will change in your relationships, and what won't.
Be clear about any decisions you can't discuss with them yet.
opening: "Things are a bit different now I'm managing the team, and I wanted to talk about how we make it work."

sayIt.line: I know it might feel strange that I'm now your manager. It does for me too.
I'll be fair and consistent with everyone, which means some things will need to be different from before.
What would help you most from me as your manager?

during: Acknowledge the change openly.
Ask about their goals and what they need from you.
Explain how you'll work: one-to-ones, decisions, and how to raise issues.
Be clear that you'll treat everyone fairly.

responses.theySay: "I thought I should have got the job."
responses.youCould: Acknowledge their disappointment without debating the decision. Ask about their career goals and how you can support them.
Agree that your role has changed, and explain why you need to be consistent with everyone.

donts: Don't overcompensate by being too strict or too relaxed.
Don't share confidential information with former close colleagues.
Don't avoid difficult conversations because of a friendship.
hrTriggers: A former peer raises a grievance about your appointment or how you manage.
You need to deal with a performance or conduct issue with a close friend.
after: Hold regular one-to-ones.
Ask your own manager for support or coaching if you need it.

summary.topic: Working together now I'm your manager
summary.prompt: What you agreed about how you'll work together.
